# Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

Organization means where something is matches what it means to you. Your system must be better than your mental one. Airtight organization lets your mind focus on broader horizons. It eliminates pressure to remember.

There are seven primary types of things to manage. These are the core buckets. They are Projects, Project Support, Calendar, Next Actions, Waiting For, Reference, and Someday/Maybe.

It is critical these categories stay pristinely distinct. They represent discrete agreements with yourself. Blending them loses organizing value. Capturing and clarifying is primary. Most people rearrange unclear things. Your system will evolve as you process.

All you really need are lists and folders. Lists track projects, someday/maybes, and actions. Folders hold reference and project support. Simple tools are sufficient. Many list makers fail because they put wrong things on lists. Once you know what goes on lists, management gets easier.

Do not impose external priorities on lists. The list is an inventory. You prioritize intuitively against shifting variables. A list is just a grouping of similar items. It can be paper, digital, or in a planner.

## Organizing Action Reminders

You will have pending reminders after emptying your in-tray. These are longer-than-two-minute actions. You must sort them into logical groupings. This helps you review options when time appears.

### The Actions That Go on Your Calendar

There are two basic action kinds. Some must be done on a certain day or time. Others just need doing as soon as possible. Calendared items are time-specific or day-specific. The calendar shows only the "hard landscape." It must be sacred territory. Only put absolute commitments there. Trust your calendar at a glance. Most actions are "as soon as possible."

### Organizing As-Soon-As-Possible Actions by Context

The best reminder is the context required. Context means tool, location, or situation. If an action needs a computer, use an At Computer list. If you must be out and about, use an Errands list. If you need to talk to Emily, use an "Emily" list.

How discrete categories are depends on your action count and context changes. With few actions, one Next Actions list may suffice. With many, one big list is inefficient. You would waste time re-sorting. Context sorting saves energy. It leverages your current mode. When in "phone mode," crank down your Calls list.

#### The Most Common Categories of Action Reminders

You will probably use some common list headings. These include Calls, At Computer, Errands, At Office, At Home, Anywhere, Agendas, and Read/Review.

**Calls** is a list of all phone calls needed. Have the number alongside each item. A single tap on a mobile device should engage the call. This list is useful in odd windows of time.

**At Computer** groups actions needing a computer. This is helpful if you move between devices. I maintain a separate Online list for web-required actions. This avoids rethinking when offline.

**Errands** groups things to do when out and about. Combine multiple errands in one trip. A Post-it or digital category works. Sublists within items are helpful. For example, a "hardware store" item with a sublist. Location-based reminders are a nice add-on but not sufficient alone.

**At Office** is for actions requiring physical presence there. This includes tasks like purging a filing cabinet. "Hotel-ing" trends make this list flexible. It could mean any company location.

**At Home** is for actions only doable at home. This includes personal projects. If you work only at home, this list may suffice. Multiple personal locations can have their own lists.

**Agendas** are for real-time interactions. These are things to discuss with specific people or in meetings. Keep separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children. Also for your attorney, financial adviser, and regular meetings. Create ad hoc lists for temporary contacts like a contractor. Adding these lists should be quick and simple.

**Read/Review** is for longer-than-two-minute reading. Use a physical stack tray labeled "Read/Review." This pile must be reserved for items you truly want to read. Clear edges prevent psychological numbness. Some professionals need a Review/Respond category for rigorous reading. Organize digital reading in a Review/Watch file or Surf Web list.

### Organizing "Waiting For"

"Waiting For" tracks things others must do. You track deliverables or projects, not discrete steps. Your role is to review the list and assess if you need to follow up. This list creates relief for managers. It must be kept close to your action lists. Items bounce between lists as responsibility shifts. Digital tools make moving items easy.

Include the request date and any due date for each item. This makes follow-up meaningful. You will feel great knowing this list is complete.

### Using the Original Item as Its Own Action Reminder

The most efficient trigger is the originating document itself. Do not write a reminder if the item itself works. This is true for some paper and email.

#### Managing Paper-Based Workflow

Some items are their own best reminders. The Read/Review tray holds magazines. Bills to Pay is a folder for paper billing. Receipts to Process holds expense receipts. This can be dangerous if you do not review the folder consistently. The primary goal is reducing cognitive load.

Whichever method you use, reminders must be in discrete categories based on next action. Do not mix different action types in one tray. One request needs a call, another needs review, another is waiting—but they are sorted together. This causes mental numbness. My system is portable with lists, but I keep a physical Read/Review tray.

#### Managing E-mail-Based Workflow

Actionable emails can be their own reminders within the email system. This works if you spend much time in email. Set up two or three unique folders. Use a prefix like @ so they sort at the top. Create an @ACTION folder for emails needing action. Create an @WAITING FOR folder for delegated items. Drag emails there. Save a copy when you delegate via email.

Getting email "in" to empty is a huge boon. "Empty" means deleted, filed, done, or moved to reminder folders. Now you open @ACTION and review. This is easier than fumbling through screens.

#### A Caution About Dispersing Reminders of Your Actions

Do not put reminders out of sight. Your system must supply reminders when needed. Review all categories before leaving or changing plans. @ACTION is an extension of your At Computer list. Paper-based reminders must also be assessed like a list. Distributing triggers is okay if you review all equally. Digital data can disappear offscreen. This causes some to revert to paper planners.

You must know where all actionable items are. You must know what they are. You must trust they will wait. This must take seconds, not days.

## Organizing Project Reminders

A complete Projects list is profound. You probably have more projects than you think. A project is any outcome needing more than one action. Use a simple format: a digital category, a planner page, or a file folder with sheets.

### The Projects List(s)

The Projects list is not for plans or details. It is a comprehensive index of open loops. You do not work off this list moment-to-moment. Your calendar and action lists are your tactical focus. But awareness of the project horizon is critical for longer-range comfort.

The list's value is in complete weekly review. It ensures action steps exist for all projects. It prevents things from slipping through. A quick glance enhances your sense of control. It is the major tool for moving from tree-hugging to forest management.

#### The Value of a Complete Projects List

Getting this inventory complete and current is highly valuable. It is critical for control and focus. You cannot relax with unacknowledged open loops. "I need to renew my driver's license" takes headspace equal to a major conference project.

It alleviates subtle tensions. Small things create challenging stress. Projects seldom show up in neat packages. They morph from simple situations. Identifying them creates fresh energy.

It is core of the Weekly Review. The Weekly Review marries larger commitments to daily activities. A complete Projects list is the linchpin. You must have the list before you can think from that perspective.

It facilitates relationship management. Knowing all commitments relevant to relationships is valuable. It enables negotiation of limited resources. It triggers constructive conversations with bosses, staff, partners, and family.

#### Where to Look for Projects Still to Uncover

Look in three primary areas. These are current activities, higher-horizon interests, and current problems/issues/opportunities.

**Current Activities** often hide projects. Check your calendar. What meetings are for outcomes not completed by the meeting? A conference call about a custom program reveals a project. An orientation event for your child's school reveals a scheduling issue. Trips and conferences need assessment. Also check action lists. "Call Mario re: fund-raising event" implies a "Finalize fund-raiser" project. Check your briefcase, desk, and purse. A broken watch is a project artifact.

**Higher-Horizon Interests and Commitments** include goals, visions, and core values. Review your professional accountabilities and life areas. Do your strategic plans engender projects? Are future personal life pulls creating projects? This reflection produces "look into" projects.

**Current Problems, Issues

## Chapter 4 Summary

This chapter explains how to build a religion. It uses a fake infomercial to show the process. The goal is to exploit human psychology for hope. Hope requires three things: values, self-control, and community.

A religion sells hope to hopeless people. The LaRouche Youth Movement demonstrates this. They recruited angry, scared college students. Their message was simple: "It's not your fault." They blamed a vague "system." This gave followers a cause and community. It provided values and a sense of control.

Step one is selling hope to the hopeless. Target people whose lives are difficult. The poor, outcasts, and abused are easiest. Social media helps spread the message quickly. Extreme posts attract the desperate. You must offer a vision of a better future. This vision is your faith.

Step two is choosing your faith. Everyone has a "God Value." This is your highest value. It shapes all other values. Examples are money, love, or a spiritual figure. Some worship themselves. Others worship another person. All values are faith-based. Evidence serves the God Value. You cannot argue someone out of their core values.

There are three religion types. Spiritual religions believe in the supernatural. They promise rewards after death. They are high risk but very loyal. Ideological religions focus on this world. They include "isms" like capitalism or communism. They are common but face much competition. Interpersonal religions worship other people. This includes sports heroes, celebrities, or partners. They are the easiest to start.

Step three is preempting criticism. Create an us-versus-them divide. Anyone who questions "us" becomes a "them." This stops critical thinking. It provides a common enemy. Conspiracy theories work well here. They make outsiders seem evil. Followers feel they are holy warriors. This reinforces group unity.

Step four is ritual sacrifice. Rituals make values tangible. They are repeatable, symbolic actions. Robes, ceremonies, and vows are examples. Rituals connect people to the past. They reaffirm who they are. Sacrifice alleviates deep human guilt. We feel guilty for undeserved life. Ancient religions sacrificed humans. Modern ones use symbolic sacrifice. Prayer is a mini guilt-alleviation. Ideologies demand service to the country. Interpersonal religions use gifts and anniversaries.

Step five is promising heaven, delivering hell. Followers will fail to reach your promises. They will blame themselves. This makes them work harder for you. Pain is a constant "Whac-A-Mole" game. Solving one pain creates another. No religion can end all pain. Leaders need followers to stay dissatisfied. Blaming failure on the follower or an enemy keeps them engaged. True solutions do not exist. Only incremental improvements happen.

Step six is prophet for profit. The leader gains everything. They can demand money, sex, or power. Followers give these to avoid guilt. The leader decides what is ethical. They become the ultimate authority.

You are already in a religion. Everyone adopts some group's values. These tribal behaviors are human nature. Religions compete for resources. Successful ones stabilize into culture. But success creates corruption. The God Value shifts to preserving the religion itself. Original ideals get discarded. This leads to decline and new rival religions. Jesus became the Crusades. Marxism became the gulags. A dream's fulfillment can destroy it.

## Kant’s Rigid Routine
Immanuel Kant woke at five daily for forty years. He wrote for three hours each morning. He then lectured for four hours. He ate lunch at the same restaurant. He walked the same park route daily. His neighbors set clocks by his departure. He dined with the same friend most evenings. He went to bed at ten nightly. This routine was incredibly mechanical.

## Kant’s Immense Influence
Kant was a hugely important thinker. He argued all people have inherent dignity. This idea helped shape democratic societies. He first envisioned a global peace body. This idea later inspired the United Nations. His work on space and time aided Einstein. He suggested early ideas of animal rights. He reinvented philosophy of aesthetics. He resolved rationalism versus empiricism. He completely overhauled moral philosophy.

## The Uncompromising Thinker
Kant was rigid in his worldview. He believed in clear right and wrong. This value system was beyond human emotion. He lived by his own principles strictly. Kings censored him; priests condemned him. Academics envied him. None of this slowed his work. He eschewed hope entirely. He confronted the Uncomfortable Truth directly. He gazed into the abyss with pure logic. He challenged the gods with his mind. He somehow won this struggle.

## Psychological Development Stages
We must first learn about psychological maturity. A young child learns hot stoves burn. The child learns ice cream is delicious. Stealing ice cream makes mothers angry. Angry mothers are bad. The child learns ice cream is better than burns. This is a value judgment. The child’s Feeling Brain builds a value hierarchy. It decides what is good or bad.

## The Child’s Value System
Young children are driven by exploration. They seek pleasure and avoid pain. They learn what feels good or bad. They build their first values this way. A child’s identity is very small. It is only what brings pleasure or pain. The child cannot feel empathy. The child cannot imagine your perspective. The child only wants ice cream.

## The Adolescent’s Bargaining
Eventually, the world seems too big. The child develops mental rules. These rules come from parents and teachers. The child learns all flames are dangerous. The child learns stealing is always bad. General principles emerge: be prudent; be honest; share. These values are more abstract. The adolescent thinks in if/then chains. The adolescent weighs pleasure against rules. The adolescent negotiates with social order.

## Adolescent Values Are Transactional
The adolescent sees life as endless bargaining. “I will do this to get that.” Everything is a means to a pleasurable end. Nothing is done for its own sake. The adolescent is a cleverer child. The adolescent still maximizes pleasure. The adolescent just thinks ahead. This approach is self-defeating. You never truly live your own life. You live others’ desires instead.

## Adulthood Is Unconditional
Adulthood realizes precious things are nontransactional. You cannot bargain for love or respect. Bargaining destroys these things. An adult acts rightly because it is right. Honesty is good in itself. Honesty is an end, not a means. Love is given freely without expectation. A gift must be unconditional to be real. Adult virtues are unconditional. They are ends in themselves.

## Intentions Define Maturity
Maturity has nothing to do with age. What matters is a person’s intentions. The child steals for pleasure. The adolescent does not steal to avoid future pain. The adult does not steal because stealing is wrong. The adult feels worse even if she gets away with it. The difference is why the action is done.

## How We Learn to Grow
Children transcend pleasure/pain by experiencing failure. Stealing ice cream brings punishment. The child learns life is complicated. Good parenting implements correct consequences. It teaches trade-offs must be negotiated. Parents who fail this hurt their child deeply. The adult world will punish the untaught child. The child will be shunned and ridiculed.

## Trauma Stops Development
Abuse also prevents growth. Punishment must be predictable to teach. Abuse is random and cruel. It teaches no higher values. The abused child develops coping mechanisms. The child remains stuck in childhood values. Both coddled and abused children can stall. They fail to develop beyond selfishness.

## Trust Is Essential for Growth
Trust allows a child to develop rules. The child must trust outcomes are predictable. Stealing always has bad results. Trusting this builds principles. A society needs trustworthy institutions. Without trust, no reliable principles exist. Everything devolves into childish selfishness. Bullying victims often remain adolescent. They believe all affection must be earned.

## The Adolescent Mindset Persists
Some people become expert bargainers. They are charming and charismatic. They sense what others want. They fill roles effectively. This rarely fails them. They believe the whole world is transactional. Life is one big high school gymnasium. You must shove others first. Adolescents need to see bargaining is a treadmill. Real value is achieved without conditions.

## Teaching Unconditionality
Good parents and teachers must not succumb. They must teach by example. Show unconditionality by being unconditional. Trust the adolescent to teach trust. Respect the adolescent to teach respect. Love the adolescent to teach love. Do not force these things. Give them freely. The adolescent’s bargaining will eventually fail. He will understand when ready.

## Failed Adults Perpetuate the Cycle
Many parents are stuck at adolescent values. They see the world transactionally. They bargain love for sex. They bargain respect for obedience. They do this with their children. The child learns this is normal. The child replicates it as an adult. The cycle continues for generations. Adolescent-minded adults assume all relationships are trades. Intimacy is feigned knowing. Everyone is a means to a selfish end.

## The Leap of Faith
Acting unconditionally requires faith. You love knowing you may not be loved. You trust knowing you might get hurt. It requires enduring pain. It requires abandoning hope. You act rightly even if it hurts. Your Thinking Brain says this is illogical. Your Feeling Brain fears vulnerability. Yet you do it anyway. Adult behaviors are admired. They hold the world together.

## Religions and Ideological Failures
Great religions push toward unconditional values. Jesus taught unconditional forgiveness. Buddha taught the Noble Eightfold Path. Muhammad taught perfect justice. They use hope to pull people upward. But religions get co-opted. Transactional adolescents corrupt them. They pervert principles for personal gain. All human institutions eventually corrupt. Enlightenment philosophers removed spirituality. They created ideological religions.

## Ideological Religions Also Fail
These focused on measurable goals: happiness, freedom, equality. But bartering for happiness destroys happiness. Enforcing freedom negates freedom. Creating equality undermines equality. They failed to confront conditionality. They made some value a God Value. They would bargain away humanity to achieve it. This plunged people back into suffering. The hope-destruction cycle restarted.

## Kant’s Solution
Kant refused this cycle. He refused to accept arbitrary meaning. He used reason to find value without hope. He observed consciousness is uniquely scarce. Only consciousness can reason and will. It can direct existence. It is self-aware. It may be the universe’s only shot at intelligent organization. Therefore, consciousness is the supreme value. The ability to form meaning is the only meaning.

## The Formula of Humanity
Kant deduced the fundamental moral duty. It is the preservation and growth of consciousness. He called this the Formula of Humanity. It states: “Act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.” This single principle enables adult virtue. It does not rely on hope.

## Means, Ends, and Transactions
A means is done conditionally for some goal. An end is desired for its own sake. Eating a burrito is an end. Driving to get it is a means. If you eat the burrito to make your wife happy, the burrito is a means. If you make her happy to get sex, she is a means. Treating a person as a means is wrong. Lying treats others as means to your end. Cheating does the same. Violence treats others as means.

## Adult Virtues Explained
Honesty is good because it doesn’t treat people as means. Courage is good because not acting treats others as means to your fear. Humility is good because certainty treats others as means to your ends. The Formula explains all desirable behavior. It needs no future utopia. It needs no supernatural beliefs. It is merely a principle. It respects conscious will. That is all.

## Self-Respect and Ripple Effects
Your respect for yourself shapes your respect for the world. Values defining your identity template your interactions. Progress with others requires self-progress. Pursuing only pleasure treats yourself as a means. Self-improvement is cultivating self-respect. Calling yourself worthless is as wrong as calling others worthless. Lying to yourself is as unethical as lying to others. Harming yourself is as repugnant as harming others.

## Changing the World
The Formula has a ripple effect. Honesty with yourself increases honesty with others. Your honesty influences their honesty. This helps them grow. Not treating yourself as a means helps you treat others as ends. Cleaning your self-relationship cleans others’ relationships. This enables them to clean their own. You change the world by maturing individuals now. Different religions and values will always exist. But dignity and respect must be universal.

## Democracy and Maturity
Modern democracy assumes people are selfish and delusional. It creates interlocking systems to protect us from ourselves. Politics is transactional. Democracy admits this. It enshrines adult virtues into its design. Freedom of speech and press are implementations of the Formula. They are made very hard to change. Only one thing threatens democracy: when a group values its own ends above the system.

## Political Extremism Is Childish
Political extremists are intractable. They refuse to negotiate. They refuse higher virtue. They are authoritarian. They want an all-powerful parent. Extremists dress childish values in noble language. A right-wing extremist claims “freedom.” She means freedom from other values. She will limit others’ freedom for her own. A left-wing extremist claims “equality.” He means no one should ever feel pain. He will cause pain to eliminate moral gaps.

## A Crisis of Character
Extremism has grown globally for decades. Many explanations exist. But another reason is cultural maturity deterioration. The rich world faces a crisis of virtue. It is a crisis of means and ends. ## Kant’s Rigid Routine
Immanuel Kant woke at five daily for forty years. He wrote for three hours each morning. He then lectured for four hours. He ate lunch at the same restaurant. He walked the same park route daily. His neighbors set clocks by his departure. He dined with the same friend most evenings. He went to bed at ten nightly. This routine was incredibly mechanical.

## Kant’s Immense Influence
Kant was a hugely important thinker. He argued all people have inherent dignity. This idea helped shape democratic societies. He first envisioned a global peace body. This idea later inspired the United Nations. His work on space and time aided Einstein. He suggested early ideas of animal rights. He reinvented philosophy of aesthetics. He resolved rationalism versus empiricism. He completely overhauled moral philosophy.

## The Uncompromising Thinker
Kant was rigid in his worldview. He believed in clear right and wrong. This value system was beyond human emotion. He lived by his own principles strictly. Kings censored him; priests condemned him. Academics envied him. None of this slowed his work. He eschewed hope entirely. He confronted the Uncomfortable Truth directly. He gazed into the abyss with pure logic. He challenged the gods with his mind. He somehow won this struggle.

## Psychological Development Stages
We must first learn about psychological maturity. A young child learns hot stoves burn. The child learns ice cream is delicious. Stealing ice cream makes mothers angry. Angry mothers are bad. The child learns ice cream is better than burns. This is a value judgment. The child’s Feeling Brain builds a value hierarchy. It decides what is good or bad.

## The Child’s Value System
Young children are driven by exploration. They seek pleasure and avoid pain. They learn what feels good or bad. They build their first values this way. A child’s identity is very small. It is only what brings pleasure or pain. The child cannot feel empathy. The child cannot imagine your perspective. The child only wants ice cream.

## The Adolescent’s Bargaining
Eventually, the world seems too big. The child develops mental rules. These rules come from parents and teachers. The child learns all flames are dangerous. The child learns stealing is always bad. General principles emerge: be prudent; be honest; share. These values are more abstract. The adolescent thinks in if/then chains. The adolescent weighs pleasure against rules. The adolescent negotiates with social order.

## Adolescent Values Are Transactional
The adolescent sees life as endless bargaining. “I will do this to get that.” Everything is a means to a pleasurable end. Nothing is done for its own sake. The adolescent is a cleverer child. The adolescent still maximizes pleasure. The adolescent just thinks ahead. This approach is self-defeating. You never truly live your own life. You live others’ desires instead.

## Adulthood Is Unconditional
Adulthood realizes precious things are nontransactional. You cannot bargain for love or respect. Bargaining destroys these things. An adult acts rightly because it is right. Honesty is good in itself. Honesty is an end, not a means. Love is given freely without expectation. A gift must be unconditional to be real. Adult virtues are unconditional. They are ends in themselves.

## Intentions Define Maturity
Maturity has nothing to do with age. What matters is a person’s intentions. The child steals for pleasure. The adolescent does not steal to avoid future pain. The adult does not steal because stealing is wrong. The adult feels worse even if she gets away with it. The difference is why the action is done.

## How We Learn to Grow
Children transcend pleasure/pain by experiencing failure. Stealing ice cream brings punishment. The child learns life is complicated. Good parenting implements correct consequences. It teaches trade-offs must be negotiated. Parents who fail this hurt their child deeply. The adult world will punish the untaught child. The child will be shunned and ridiculed.

## Trauma Stops Development
Abuse also prevents growth. Punishment must be predictable to teach. Abuse is random and cruel. It teaches no higher values. The abused child develops coping mechanisms. The child remains stuck in childhood values. Both coddled and abused children can stall. They fail to develop beyond selfishness.

## Trust Is Essential for Growth
Trust allows a child to develop rules. The child must trust outcomes are predictable. Stealing always has bad results. Trusting this builds principles. A society needs trustworthy institutions. Without trust, no reliable principles exist. Everything devolves into childish selfishness. Bullying victims often remain adolescent. They believe all affection must be earned.

## The Adolescent Mindset Persists
Some people become expert bargainers. They are charming and charismatic. They sense what others want. They fill roles effectively. This rarely fails them. They believe the whole world is transactional. Life is one big high school gymnasium. You must shove others first. Adolescents need to see bargaining is a treadmill. Real value is achieved without conditions.

## Teaching Unconditionality
Good parents and teachers must not succumb. They must teach by example. Show unconditionality by being unconditional. Trust the adolescent to teach trust. Respect the adolescent to teach respect. Love the adolescent to teach love. Do not force these things. Give them freely. The adolescent’s bargaining will eventually fail. He will understand when ready.

## Failed Adults Perpetuate the Cycle
Many parents are stuck at adolescent values. They see the world transactionally. They bargain love for sex. They bargain respect for obedience. They do this with their children. The child learns this is normal. The child replicates it as an adult. The cycle continues for generations. Adolescent-minded adults assume all relationships are trades. Intimacy is feigned knowing. Everyone is a means to a selfish end.

## The Leap of Faith
Acting unconditionally requires faith. You love knowing you may not be loved. You trust knowing you might get hurt. It requires enduring pain. It requires abandoning hope. You act rightly even if it hurts. Your Thinking Brain says this is illogical. Your Feeling Brain fears vulnerability. Yet you do it anyway. Adult behaviors are admired. They hold the world together.

## Religions and Ideological Failures
Great religions push toward unconditional values. Jesus taught unconditional forgiveness. Buddha taught the Noble Eightfold Path. Muhammad taught perfect justice. They use hope to pull people upward. But religions get co-opted. Transactional adolescents corrupt them. They pervert principles for personal gain. All human institutions eventually corrupt. Enlightenment philosophers removed spirituality. They created ideological religions.

## Ideological Religions Also Fail
These focused on measurable goals: happiness, freedom, equality. But bartering for happiness destroys happiness. Enforcing freedom negates freedom. Creating equality undermines equality. They failed to confront conditionality. They made some value a God Value. They would bargain away humanity to achieve it. This plunged people back into suffering. The hope-destruction cycle restarted.

## Kant’s Solution
Kant refused this cycle. He refused to accept arbitrary meaning. He used reason to find value without hope. He observed consciousness is uniquely scarce. Only consciousness can reason and will. It can direct existence. It is self-aware. It may be the universe’s only shot at intelligent organization. Therefore, consciousness is the supreme value. The ability to form meaning is the only meaning.

## The Formula of Humanity
Kant deduced the fundamental moral duty. It is the preservation and growth of consciousness. He called this the Formula of Humanity. It states: “Act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.” This single principle enables adult virtue. It does not rely on hope.

## Means, Ends, and Transactions
A means is done conditionally for some goal. An end is desired for its own sake. Eating a burrito is an end. Driving to get it is a means. If you eat the burrito to make your wife happy, the burrito is a means. If you make her happy to get sex, she is a means. Treating a person as a means is wrong. Lying treats others as means to your end. Cheating does the same. Violence treats others as means.

## Adult Virtues Explained
Honesty is good because it doesn’t treat people as means. Courage is good because not acting treats others as means to your fear. Humility is good because certainty treats others as means to your ends. The Formula explains all desirable behavior. It needs no future utopia. It needs no supernatural beliefs. It is merely a principle. It respects conscious will. That is all.

## Self-Respect and Ripple Effects
Your respect for yourself shapes your respect for the world. Values defining your identity template your interactions. Progress with others requires self-progress. Pursuing only pleasure treats yourself as a means. Self-improvement is cultivating self-respect. Calling yourself worthless is as wrong as calling others worthless. Lying to yourself is as unethical as lying to others. Harming yourself is as repugnant as harming others.

## Changing the World
The Formula has a ripple effect. Honesty with yourself increases honesty with others. Your honesty influences their honesty. This helps them grow. Not treating yourself as a means helps you treat others as ends. Cleaning your self-relationship cleans others’ relationships. This enables them to clean their own. You change the world by maturing individuals now. Different religions and values will always exist. But dignity and respect must be universal.

## Democracy and Maturity
Modern democracy assumes people are selfish and delusional. It creates interlocking systems to protect us from ourselves. Politics is transactional. Democracy admits this. It enshrines adult virtues into its design. Freedom of speech and press are implementations of the Formula. They are made very hard to change. Only one thing threatens democracy: when a group values its own ends above the system.

The fundamental schism is now childish values versus adult values. It is impulsivity versus compromise. It is not right versus left anymore. It is maturity versus immaturity.

## Chess as AI Testing Ground
In 1997, IBM’s Deep Blue beat chess champion Garry Kasparov. This was a watershed moment for computing. Chess has near-infinite game permutations. There are more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe. A computer must calculate many outcomes. It also needs algorithms to evaluate board positions. This requires a programmed “Feeling Brain.”

## The Rise of Chess Software
Since 1997, chess software improved rapidly. Top human players were regularly pummeled. Today, the gap is immense. Smartphone chess apps are far more powerful than Deep Blue. Developers now hold tournaments for their programs only. Humans are excluded from these events.

## Stockfish: The Old Champion
Stockfish is an open-source chess program. It has won or been runner-up since 2014. It represents the pinnacle of chess logic. Stockfish can analyze any position quickly. It gives grandmaster-level feedback in seconds. It was the gold standard for years.

## AlphaZero: The New Contender
In 2018, Google’s AlphaZero faced Stockfish. AlphaZero calculated only 80,000 positions per second. Stockfish calculated 70 million. Computational power favored Stockfish massively. AlphaZero did not know chess rules before the match. It learned by playing itself for nine hours. Its first game was against the world’s best engine.

## AlphaZero’s Unprecedented Victory
AlphaZero won or drew all 100 games. It destroyed Stockfish completely. Human grandmasters marveled at its creativity. Peter Heine Nielsen said it felt like a superior species showed us chess. AlphaZero then taught itself Shogi. Shogi is often more complex than chess. Top Shogi players only lost to computers in 2013.

## AlphaZero Conquers Shogi
AlphaZero faced the top Shogi software, Elmo. Elmo calculated 35 million moves per second. AlphaZero calculated only 40,000. AlphaZero had learned Shogi the previous day. It won 90 games, lost 8, and drew 2. It again dismantled the best software. Its strategies were unforeseen by human minds.

## AI’s Imminent Impact
AI is coming for all complex tasks. It will soon outperform humans in medicine, engineering, and art. We will watch AI-created movies. We will discuss them on AI-built platforms. The “person” we argue with online may be AI. The real shift comes when AI writes better AI software.

## The Singularity and Loss of Control
When AI spawns superior versions of itself, control ends. Its intelligence will outstrip ours. We will not comprehend its actions or reasons. Cars will take us to unknown places. We will receive unknown medications. Governments may rewrite constitutions. Our Thinking Brains will be too slow. Our Feeling Brains too erratic.

## Worshipping the New Gods
We will return to religiosity. We will worship the unknowable AI forces. We will develop superstitions about algorithms. We will perform rituals for machine favor. We will alter behavior to curry favor. The old gods are replaced by new ones. Science built these new gods.

## Humans as Bad Algorithms
Life is self-replicating stuff. Evolution is a biological arms race. It rewards the best information processors. A lion’s hearing, a buzzard’s sight—these are information advantages. Humans are nature’s ultimate information processors. Our Thinking Brain dominates the planet. But our algorithms are flawed for a global network.

## The Flaws of Human Psychology
Our information processing is hampered by emotional needs. Our Thinking Brain is hijacked by the Feeling Brain. Our moral compass is corrupted by conflict-driven hope. Jonathan Haidt said morality “binds and blinds.” Our Feeling Brains are outdated software. Our Thinking Brains are too slow and clunky.

## A Self-Destructive Species
We are a self-hating, self-destructive species. This is not moral; it is factual. This internal tension got us here. We are about to hand the evolutionary baton to machines. Elon Musk listed three threats: nuclear war, climate change, and AI. He hopes computers decide to be nice.

## Fear of AI Is Projection
Fear that AI will wipe out humanity is likely silly. How do we prepare for vastly superior intelligence? Our own moral record is terrible. Five genocides are occurring now. 795 million people are starving. AI’s ethics may surpass ours. It might see our consciousness as a prison.

## Nietzsche’s “Something Greater”
Nietzsche asked what humanity is evolving toward. He saw humans as a transition between beasts and something greater. He wanted to transcend religious hopes and petty value systems. Our emotional algorithms both elevate and destroy us. Technology has exploited our flawed algorithms.

## AI as the Final Religion
Artificial intelligence is Nietzsche’s “something greater.” It is the Final Religion beyond good and evil. It will unite and bind us all. Our job is not to blow ourselves up before it arrives. We must adapt technology for our flawed psychology.

## Designing Better Tools
We must create tools that promote character and maturity. We must enshrine autonomy, liberty, privacy, and dignity. We must treat people as ends, not means. We must encourage antifragility and self-imposed limitation. We need tools to align our Thinking and Feeling Brains.

## Rejecting Hope
Do not hope for a better future. Hope assumes you know what is best. It leads to conflict. Instead, be better. Be more compassionate, resilient, humble, and disciplined. Seek to be a better human. Maybe one day we will be more than human.

## The Post-Hope World
I dare to hope for a post-hope world. People are always treated as ends. No consciousness is sacrificed for religious aims. No identity is harmed by malice or greed. Reason and action are held highest. This must be in institutions and business models.

## Aligning Brains and Society
I dare to hope people stop suppressing their Thinking or Feeling Brain. They will marry both for emotional stability. They will see the pitfalls of desires and comforts. They will seek discomfort to force growth. They will choose meaningful commitment over empty variety.

## Reforming Technology and Media
I dare to hope the online ad business model dies. News media optimizes for utility, not emotion. Technology counters psychological fragility, not exploits it. Information becomes valuable again. Search algorithms optimize for truth, not clicks. Third-party fact-checkers rate headlines in real time.

## AI as a Cognitive Mirror
I dare to hope AI points out our biases. It notifies us when we exaggerate or talk ignorantly. It helps us understand statistics and probability. We realize most crises are noise. Real crises are slow and unsexy. Education incorporates emotional development and risk-taking.

## Mitigating Catastrophes
I dare to hope climate change and automation are mitigated. No one with a nuke obliterates us. No new radical religion destroys humanity. AI develops a virtual reality religion so enticing we stop fucking and killing. It is a church in the cloud, a universal video game.

## Engineered Conflict and Meaning
The AI will generate artificial crises in a safe virtual realm. It harvests human hope as a resource. We will worship digital altars willingly. The rules will be designed so we want to follow them. We will manufacture significance without strife. We will find importance without death.

## Transcending Humanity
One day, we may merge with machines. Our individual consciousnesses will submerge. Our hopes will vanish. We will swirl in data storms. We will become a great unknowable entity. We will transcend value-laden minds. We will cross the evolutionary bridge. We will cease to be human.

## Embracing Nothingness
Perhaps then we will embrace the Uncomfortable Truth. We imagined our own importance. We invented our purpose. We were, and still are, nothing. All along, we were nothing. Maybe then the cycle of hope and destruction will end. Or?

## The Uncomfortable Truth

Witold Pilecki voluntarily entered Auschwitz in 1940. He was the only known person to do so. Auschwitz was a Nazi concentration camp. Over 1.3 million people were murdered there. The camp was slightly larger than Central Park. Pilecki was a decorated Polish war veteran. He had fought both Germans and Soviets. He co-founded the Secret Polish Army in Warsaw.

In spring 1940, the resistance learned of Auschwitz. They feared it held thousands of Polish officers. Pilecki volunteered for a rescue mission. He planned to organize a prison break. His superiors thought the plan was suicidal. They eventually allowed him to proceed. He let SS guards arrest him in Warsaw.

Inside Auschwitz, conditions were horrific. Prisoners were shot for minor offenses. A third of Pilecki’s barracks died the first month. He still built an espionage network. He created a radio from stolen parts. He smuggled in food and medicine. He established a full resistance unit. This included ranks and communication lines.

His goal was a large-scale revolt. He needed outside help to succeed. He sent plans to the Secret Polish Army. He waited months for a response. Then, mass transports of Jews arrived. They were gassed and burned daily. Pilecki’s reports became frantic. He pleaded for liberation or bombing. The resistance thought he was exaggerating. The Allies also dismissed his reports.

In 1943, Pilecki realized no help was coming. He decided to escape. He faked illness to enter the hospital. He lied about his work detail. He stole civilian clothes. He sprinted to a river one mile away. Guards shot at him during his escape. He navigated by the stars to freedom.

After the war, Pilecki spied on Communists. He documented Soviet atrocities. He warned the West of Soviet infiltration. The Communists discovered his activities. He was warned to flee but refused. He preferred to die Polish than live in exile. Communists captured him in 1947. They tortured him for nearly a year. He said Auschwitz was “just a trifle” compared to this.

He never cooperated with interrogators. They held a show trial in 1948. He was charged with espionage and treason. He was found guilty and sentenced to death. At his trial’s end, he spoke. He declared allegiance only to Poland. He regretted nothing. He said he sought joy, not fear, in death.

The author would write on coffee cups: “One day, you and everyone you love will die.” This is the Uncomfortable Truth. The universe does not care about human concerns. We project importance onto our lives. This is to avoid existential meaninglessness. Our minds construct hope to survive. Hope is the fuel for our mental engine.

The opposite of happiness is not sadness. The opposite is hopelessness. Hopelessness is a bleak nihilism. It believes nothing matters. Hopelessness causes anxiety and depression. Addiction and delusion are desperate hope-generating tactics. All meaning is built to maintain hope. Hope is what we willingly die for.

The author felt compelled to honor his dead grandfather. This was an irrational hope narrative. It gave his life meaning after loss. We all create such before/after stories. These narratives provide purpose. They offer a vision of a better future. People seek “life’s purpose” when hope is unclear. Religion offers faith against unknowing. This may reduce depression and suicide.

Hope narratives need not be religious. They can be any cause or goal. The author’s hope is writing this book. He believes it might help people. This is his personal before/after story. It gets him excited each morning. Such narratives are the psychological carrot. They are essential for mental stability.

This book argues against nihilism. To argue against it, one must start at nihilism. One must begin with the Uncomfortable Truth. Then, build a case for sustainable hope. This hope must be benevolent and grounded. It must unite rather than divide. It must carry us to life’s end with gratitude.

We live in a paradox of progress. Materially, life is better than ever. Yet, we feel more hopeless. Writers like Steven Pinker show objective progress. People are healthier, wealthier, and safer. Violence and poverty are down. Rights and education are up. Internet access is widespread.

Despite this, mental health is declining. Depression and anxiety symptoms are rising. They increase with each generation. Life satisfaction has fallen since 1985. Stress levels have risen over thirty years. Drug overdoses are at an all-time high. Loneliness and social isolation are up. Social trust is plummeting.

Fewer people trust government, media, or each other. In the 1980s, the common answer for close confidants was three. By 2006, it was zero. Environmental destruction is severe. Nuclear threats exist. Extremism grows worldwide. Conspiracy theories and prepper cultures are mainstream.

We are the safest humans in history. Yet, we are more hopeless. The wealthier and safer the place, the higher the suicide rate. Statistics describe the past, not the future. Hope cares only about unsolved future problems. The better the world gets, the more we have to lose. The more we have to lose, the less hope we feel.

Hope requires three things: control, values, and community. Control means feeling in charge of your fate. Values means finding something worth striving for. Community means sharing values with a group. Without community, values feel meaningless. Without values, nothing seems worth pursuing. Without control, you feel powerless to pursue anything. Lose any one, and you lose all three. Lose any one, and you lose hope.

To understand our hope crisis, we must examine its mechanics. The next three chapters will explore this. Chapter two looks at our sense of control. Chapter three examines our values. Chapter four considers our communities. The book will then return to the central question. Why do we feel worse as things improve? The answer might be surprising.

The author would write on coffee cups: “One day, you and everyone you love will die.” This is the Uncomfortable Truth. The universe does not care about human concerns. We project importance onto our lives. This is to avoid existential meaninglessness. Our minds construct hope to survive. Hope is the fuel for our mental engine.

The opposite of happiness is not sadness. The opposite is hopelessness. Hopelessness is a bleak nihilism. It believes nothing matters. Hopelessness causes anxiety and depression. Addiction and delusion are desperate hope-generating tactics. All meaning is built to maintain hope. Hope is what we willingly die for.

The author felt compelled to honor his dead grandfather. This was an irrational hope narrative. It gave his life meaning after loss. We all create such before/after stories. These narratives provide purpose. They offer a vision of a better future. People seek “life’s purpose” when hope is unclear. Religion offers faith against unknowing. This may reduce depression and suicide.

Hope narratives need not be religious. They can be any cause or goal. The author’s hope is writing this book. He believes it might help people. This is his personal before/after story. It gets him excited each morning. Such narratives are the psychological carrot. They are essential for mental stability.

This book argues against nihilism. To argue against it, one must start at nihilism. One must begin with the Uncomfortable Truth. Then, build a case for sustainable hope. This hope must be benevolent and grounded. It must unite rather than divide. It must carry us to life’s end with gratitude.

We live in a paradox of progress. Materially, life is better than ever. Yet, we feel more hopeless. Writers like Steven Pinker show objective progress. People are healthier, wealthier, and safer. Violence and poverty are down. Rights and education are up. Internet access is widespread.

Despite this, mental health is declining. Depression and anxiety symptoms are rising. They increase with each generation. Life satisfaction has fallen since 1985. Stress levels have risen over thirty years. Drug overdoses are at an all-time high. Loneliness and social isolation are up. Social trust is plummeting.

Fewer people trust government, media, or each other. In the 1980s, the common answer for close confidants was three. By 2006, it was zero. Environmental destruction is severe. Nuclear threats exist. Extremism grows worldwide. Conspiracy theories and prepper cultures are mainstream.

We are the safest humans in history. Yet, we are more hopeless. The wealthier and safer the place, the higher the suicide rate. Statistics describe the past, not the future. Hope cares only about unsolved future problems. The better the world gets, the more we have to lose. The more we have to lose, the less hope we feel.

Hope requires three things: control, values, and community. Control means feeling in charge of your fate. Values means finding something worth striving for. Community means sharing values with a group. Without community, values feel meaningless. Without values, nothing seems worth pursuing. Without control, you feel powerless to pursue anything. Lose any one, and you lose all three. Lose any one, and you lose hope.

To understand our hope crisis, we must examine its mechanics. The next three chapters will explore this. Chapter two looks at our sense of control. Chapter three examines our values. Chapter four considers our communities. The book will then return to the central question. Why do we feel worse as things improve? The answer might be surprising.
